opencl.verdict: NEGATIVE -- structural, not a tuning failure
opencl.why: OpenCL does not expose DeterministicForces; the CPU platform does and core/amber.py sets it true, which is what makes the pinned golden reproducible.  Bitwise reproducibility is unavailable by construction.

core_map.note: ranked with the AMBER workload itself, not a proxy kernel.  A GBn2 minimisation is bandwidth-bound and ranks the cores differently from a float64 spin loop (1.24x, no pattern) or a cache-resident matmul (1.7x, no pattern).  With the real workload the split is clean and 4/4.
core_map.implication: the machine is 6.43 fast-core-equivalents, not 8.  The bench sweep's saturation at ~3.9 effective workers is the P-core COUNT, not the memory wall, which bites later at w8.

predicted_cpu_inflation_if_work_spreads_.CORRECTION: this block previously called mean(1/rel) 'the floor'.  It is not.  It is the prediction for ONE scheduling regime -- equal COUNT of structures per core -- and the old dispatcher happened to be in it (contiguous equal-count chunks).  There are two regimes and each has its own prediction; both are now measured and both land.

regime_equal_count_per_core.applies_to: static contiguous equal-count chunks (the old dispatcher)

regime_equal_wall_per_core.applies_to: any DYNAMIC dispatch: every core stays busy the same wall time, so fast cores complete MORE structures and the per-structure CPU average is weighted toward them.  This is the true floor at w8.

predicted_cpu_inflation_if_work_spreads_.conclusion: The core map is confirmed TWICE, by two schedules that sit in different regimes and each land on their own prediction to within 0.7%.  The residual excess over the dynamic floor is +0.67%, about 8.6 CPU-s of 1611.59 -- so there is no memory-bandwidth contention left in AMBER at all.  A concurrency cap would idle cores to relieve nothing.

core_map.methodological_finding: A PROXY KERNEL DID NOT ADD ERROR, IT REMOVED THE SIGNAL.  Two independent proxy rankings of these cores -- a float64 spin loop (1.24x spread) and a cache-resident matmul (1.7x spread) -- both found NO 4/4 pattern and both led to the conclusion that core heterogeneity was not the constraint.  The real workload finds a clean 4/4 split at 1.67x that accounts for AMBER's entire w8 inflation to 0.03%.  The reason is mechanistic rather than statistical: a cache-resident kernel and a bandwidth-bound one load different parts of the machine, so they do not merely rank the cores noisily, they rank them by a different quantity.  Rank hardware with the workload whose cost you are trying to explain.  (The same lesson this project already recorded when a decoy-bank ranker failed to transfer to real pools.)

affinity.verdict: NEGATIVE -- pinning to the fast cores is worse than letting the OS place
conclusions: B reproduces the bench sweep's +14.9% at w4 (+14.4%) in a pure AMBER harness with a tiny footprint and RAM nowhere near the gate -- so the AMBER inflation is NOT page pressure and NOT the window-bank footprint.

D is +40.7% with exactly zero contention: one process, one slow core.  Core heterogeneity alone is a LARGER effect than the entire w4 regression, so the w4 inflation is dominated by placement onto slow cores, not by L3 contention.

C is worse than B on both CPU (+24% vs +14%) and wall (3.3x), reproduced twice.  Packing four workers onto the four P-cores makes them contend with each other and with the OS threads that also prefer P-cores, and forbids the E-cores entirely.  There is no cheap bit-identical affinity fix.

bit_identity.note: one distinct energy per target across every arm; placement cannot change arithmetic, and this verifies it rather than assuming it

threads.verdict: t2 is a REGRESSION; t4 is 1.97x wall for 1.65x the CPU-seconds
threads.corrects: the feasibility model assumed AMBER thread speedups of 1.5 at t2 and 2.2 at t4.  t2 measures 0.908 -- slower than t1 -- which falsifies the recommended w4 x t2 hybrid.  t4's 1.97 is close to the assumed 2.2 but costs 1.65x the CPU-seconds, and the feasibility bound counts CPU-seconds, so threading makes the BOUND worse while improving wall only where cores would otherwise sit idle.
threads.stronger_reason_to_reject: The wall numbers alone kill t2, but the decisive objection is that OpenMM's thread count changes the RESULT and not only the speed: _calibrate_hydrogens inherits the thread count and settles in a different minimum, moving the energy by ~144 kcal/mol.  So a w4 x t2 arm would have to be restated as a tolerance, while w8 x t1 is both faster and bit-identical -- the trade was never live.  (Measured by the bench agent; consistent with the -3.4e-2 kcal/mol per-structure deviation measured here, which is the minimisation alone with the calibration held fixed.)

ceiling.note: wall >= CPU_work / effective_cores.  Dividing by 8 is 24% optimistic on this box; the AMBER-workload capacity is 6.426 fastest-core-equivalents. NOTE: the per-structure inflation floor depends on the SCHEDULE (1.2908 static equal-count, 1.2449 dynamic); the core-equivalents figure 6.426 does not.
